Full marks may be obtained for answers to ALL questions. Mathematical formulae booklets published by the Board are allowed. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving the answer at each stage. Calculators are allowed. Start each question on a fresh page.
incertitudes: Question 6 (i) : le sujet imprime f(x) = x^2 - 2 pour 0 <= x < 2 et f(x) = 4 - x pour 2 <= x <= 4 (borne 4 incluse) avec f de période 4 ; cela est contradictoire en x = 4, car f(4) = 0 d'après la 2e ligne mais f(4) = f(0) = -2 par périodicité. Le corrigé prend la définition sur [0, 4) prolongée par périodicité (f(4k) = -2, cercle vide en hauteur 0 à gauche des multiples de 4) et le signale ; f(19) = f(3) = 1 et f(-43) = f(1) = -1 ne dépendent pas de cette convention.
Question 6 (i)(b) : tracé demandé, aucune figure imprimée ; le corrigé décrit la courbe par intervalles avec les points clés (tableau).

questions.enonce_markdown:
The function $f$ is periodic with period $4$. Given that

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 - 2 & \text{for } 0 \le x < 2, \\ 4 - x & \text{for } 2 \le x \le 4, \end{cases}$$

(a) evaluate $f(19)$ and $f(-43)$,

(b) sketch the graph of $f(x)$ in the range $-4 \le x < 8$. (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Periodic with period $4$ means $f(x + 4) = f(x)$ for all $x$, so $f(x) = f(x - 4k)$ for any integer $k$. Every value is therefore found from the formula on $[0, 4)$.

**(a)** $19 = 4\times 4 + 3$, so $f(19) = f(3)$. Since $2 \le 3 \le 4$, use $4 - x$:

$$f(19) = f(3) = 4 - 3 = 1.$$

$-43 = 4\times(-11) + 1$, so $f(-43) = f(1)$. Since $0 \le 1 < 2$, use $x^2 - 2$:

$$f(-43) = f(1) = 1^2 - 2 = -1.$$

$$\boxed{f(19) = 1, \qquad f(-43) = -1}$$

**(b)** First draw one period, $0 \le x < 4$, then repeat it by translating by $\pm 4$.

- On $[0, 2)$: the parabola $y = x^2 - 2$, from $(0, -2)$ through $(1, -1)$ and $(\sqrt2, 0)$ to the point $(2, 2)$ (approached as $x \to 2^-$).
- On $[2, 4)$: the straight line $y = 4 - x$, from $(2, 2)$ through $(3, 1)$ down towards $(4, 0)$ (open end).

The two pieces meet at $(2, 2)$ since $2^2 - 2 = 2 = 4 - 2$, so $f$ is continuous at $x = 2$ (and at $x = 6$, $x = -2$). At $x = 0$ the value is $f(0) = -2$ but the limit from the left is $4 - 4 = 0$ (the left-hand piece is the line near $x = 4$ translated), so there is a **jump** of $2$ at every multiple of $4$.

Pieces in the required range $-4 \le x < 8$:

| interval | rule | key points |
|---|---|---|
| $[-4, -2)$ | $(x+4)^2 - 2$ | $(-4, -2)$ filled; $(-3, -1)$; $(-4+\sqrt2,\,0) \approx (-2.59,\,0)$; reaching $(-2, 2)$ |
| $[-2, 0)$ | $-x$ | $(-2, 2)$; $(-1, 1)$; towards $(0, 0)$ (open circle) |
| $[0, 2)$ | $x^2 - 2$ | $(0, -2)$ filled; $(1, -1)$; $(\sqrt2, 0)$; reaching $(2, 2)$ |
| $[2, 4)$ | $4 - x$ | $(2, 2)$; $(3, 1)$; towards $(4, 0)$ (open circle) |
| $[4, 6)$ | $(x-4)^2 - 2$ | $(4, -2)$ filled; $(5, -1)$; $(4+\sqrt2,\,0) \approx (5.41,\,0)$; reaching $(6, 2)$ |
| $[6, 8)$ | $8 - x$ | $(6, 2)$; $(7, 1)$; towards $(8, 0)$ (open circle, $x = 8$ excluded) |

Description of the sketch: a repeating "hill-and-slope" pattern of period $4$. Each period starts at a filled dot at height $-2$ (at $x = -4, 0, 4$), rises along a parabola through $(\sqrt2, 0)$ to the peak $(2, 2)$ (at $x = -2, 2, 6$), then falls along a straight line to an open circle at height $0$ (at $x = 0, 4, 8$), after which the graph jumps down to the filled dot at $-2$. The values of $f$ always lie in $[-2, 2]$, and the graph crosses the $x$-axis at $x = -4+\sqrt2,\ \sqrt2,\ 4+\sqrt2$.

Check against part (a): the sketch gives $f(3) = 1$ and $f(1) = -1$, as found.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A relation $\mathcal{R}$ is defined on $\mathbb{Z}$, the set of integers, by $a\mathcal{R}b$ if and only if $(a + b)$ is even.

Show that $\mathcal{R}$ is an equivalence relation. (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A relation is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Let $a, b, c \in \mathbb{Z}$.

**Reflexive.** $a + a = 2a = 2(a)$, which is even, so $a\mathcal{R}a$ for every $a \in \mathbb{Z}$.

**Symmetric.** Suppose $a\mathcal{R}b$, i.e. $a + b$ is even. Since addition is commutative, $b + a = a + b$ is even, so $b\mathcal{R}a$.

**Transitive.** Suppose $a\mathcal{R}b$ and $b\mathcal{R}c$, i.e. $a + b = 2m$ and $b + c = 2p$ for some integers $m$, $p$. Adding,

$$(a + b) + (b + c) = 2m + 2p \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a + c = 2m + 2p - 2b = 2(m + p - b),$$

and $m + p - b$ is an integer, so $a + c$ is even, i.e. $a\mathcal{R}c$.

$\mathcal{R}$ is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, hence an **equivalence relation**. $\blacksquare$

Remark: $a + b$ is even exactly when $a$ and $b$ have the same parity, so $\mathcal{R}$ partitions $\mathbb{Z}$ into two equivalence classes, the even integers and the odd integers.
